blocks.text: Rank answers a question that sounds abstract but turns out to matter constantly: how much genuinely independent, non-redundant information does a matrix actually contain? Two matrices can have the exact same shape while holding very different amounts of real information, and rank is the number that captures that difference.

blocks.alt: A matrix branching into rank, which is either full rank or rank deficient
blocks.caption: This lesson covers exactly what separates these two cases.

blocks.text: 1. What Rank Actually Counts
The rank of a matrix is the number of independent rows, or equivalently independent columns, it contains. A row is independent if it cannot be built by scaling and adding together the other rows.

This same idea applies equally well counting columns instead of rows, the rank computed either way always comes out identical, a genuinely useful fact that is not obvious at first but holds for every matrix.
Rank is always a single whole number, never a fraction or a range, and it can never be larger than the smaller of the total row count or total column count, a limit revisited directly in section 3.
2. A Row That Adds Nothing New
Consider a matrix where one row is simply a scaled copy of another. That second row carries no new information at all, it is entirely predictable once the first row is known.

blocks.alt: A 2 by 2 matrix where the second row is exactly twice the first row
blocks.caption: Even though this matrix has 2 rows, it only really contains 1 independent direction of information.

code.content:
import numpy as np
M = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(M))   # 1, not 2

blocks.text: 3. Full Rank vs Rank Deficient

A matrix has full rank when its rank equals the smaller of its row count and column count, meaning every row (or column) genuinely contributes independent information. A matrix with a lower rank than that is called rank deficient.

The smaller of row count and column count matters specifically because rank can never exceed either one. A 2 by 5 matrix, for example, can have a rank of at most 2, since there are only 2 rows available to be independent from each other in the first place, no matter how many columns exist.
3.1 Checking Two Matrices Side by Side

The third row confirms the min-of-row-and-column-count rule from earlier in this section directly: a 2 by 3 matrix can never exceed rank 2, no matter how its 3 columns are chosen, so reaching rank 2 here already means it is full rank.
4. Computing Rank in Code

code.content:
A = np.array([[1, 0, 2], [0, 1, 3], [1, 1, 5]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A))   # 2, even though A is 3 by 3

blocks.text: That result is worth noticing directly: a 3 by 3 matrix does not automatically have rank 3. Here the third row happens to equal the first row plus the second row, adding no new independent information, capping the true rank at 2.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: The matrix [[1,0,2],[0,1,3],[1,1,5]] looks full size at first glance, but its third row equals the first row plus the second row exactly, so it only reaches rank 2 even though it is a 3 by 3 matrix. Spotting that a row is a combination of two others, not just a scaled copy of one, is a subtler version of the dependency check from section 2.

blocks.text: 5. Rank and Invertibility

This connects directly to the matrix inverse lesson: a square matrix is invertible exactly when it has full rank. The singular matrix from that lesson, where one row was a multiple of another, had a rank lower than its size, which is precisely why no inverse existed for it.

code.content:
singular = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(singular))   # 1, less than 2, confirming it cannot be inverted

blocks.text: This gives a genuinely useful diagnostic habit: whenever a matrix inversion fails unexpectedly, checking its rank against its size immediately reveals whether the problem is a true mathematical impossibility, a rank deficient matrix, or something else entirely, like a numerical precision issue covered in the matrix inverse lesson.
6. Rank as True Dimensionality

A useful way to think about rank: it tells you how many genuinely independent directions a matrix worth of data actually spans, regardless of how many rows or columns it is stored with. A dataset stored as 100 columns but with a rank of only 5 is really only 5-dimensional information wearing 100 columns worth of storage.

This dimensionality reading of rank is what makes it a natural bridge between raw matrix arithmetic and the more geometric ideas covered later in this module, where dimension, basis, and independent direction all describe the same underlying structure from slightly different angles.
6.1 A Concrete Example

blocks.title: Worked scenario
blocks.content: A spreadsheet tracking length in centimeters and length in inches for the same set of objects has 2 columns but a rank of only 1, since one column is always a fixed multiple of the other. Every genuinely new measurement adds a column, but only measurements that are not simply derived from existing ones actually raise the rank.

blocks.text: 7. Where Rank Matters in AI

items: Detecting redundant features in a dataset, columns that add storage but no new independent information.

Low-rank approximation, deliberately replacing a large matrix with a lower-rank version that captures most of its important structure using far less storage, the same idea explored fully in the SVD lesson.
Diagnosing why a matrix inversion or linear system solve unexpectedly failed, a rank check is one of the first things worth trying.

blocks.text: This is also exactly why checking for highly correlated features is a standard early step in preparing data for a machine learning model, two features that are nearly perfect multiples of each other are close to rank deficient together, adding storage and computation cost without contributing proportional new information.

Compression, redundancy detection, and cheap fine tuning all turn out to be the same underlying move: find the smaller number of independent directions a large matrix truly relies on, then work with that smaller number instead of the full, inflated size.
8. Row Space, Column Space, and Null Space

Rank connects to three related ideas that come up throughout linear algebra: the row space, the set of every combination the rows can produce, the column space, the same idea for columns, and the null space, the set of every vector that the matrix crushes down to all zeros. Rank is simply the dimension of the row space, which always equals the dimension of the column space, no matter how lopsided the matrix looks.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: For the matrix [[1, 2], [2, 4]] used earlier, the null space contains any vector of the form (x, negative half x), since the matrix maps every such vector to (0, 0). This matches the rank of 1: one dimension of input gets preserved, and the remaining one dimension gets collapsed into the null space.

blocks.text: 8.1 The Rank Nullity Theorem

For a matrix with n columns, rank plus the dimension of the null space always adds up to exactly n. A 3 column matrix with rank 2 must have a 1 dimensional null space, a 3 column matrix with rank 3 has a null space containing only the zero vector. This single equation is what ties together how much information a matrix preserves versus how much it discards.
9. Rank and Systems of Linear Equations

Rank determines whether a system of linear equations has exactly one solution, no solution, or infinitely many. Comparing the rank of the coefficient matrix against the rank of the augmented matrix, the coefficient matrix with the answer column tacked on, tells you which of the three cases you are in before doing any further solving.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Comparison","What it means","Solutions"],"rows":[["rank(A) = rank(A|b) = number of unknowns","every unknown is pinned down","exactly one solution"],["rank(A) = rank(A|b) < number of unknowns","some freedom remains","infinitely many solutions"],["rank(A) < rank(A|b)","the equations contradict each other","no solution"]]}

blocks.text: This is the same rank deficiency from section 3 showing up in a practical setting: a rank deficient coefficient matrix, one with fewer independent rows than unknowns, cannot pin down every unknown uniquely on its own, so the system either has no solution or infinitely many, never exactly one.
10. Low Rank Approximation

Many real matrices are technically full rank but only barely, most of their information really lives in a much smaller number of dominant directions, with the rest being negligible noise. Replacing such a matrix with the closest matrix of a smaller, chosen rank is called low rank approximation, and it is one of the most widely used compression tricks in applied machine learning.

code.content:
import numpy as np
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
k = 2
A_approx = U[:, :k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k, :]  # closest rank-2 matrix to A

blocks.text: This is exactly the mechanism behind image compression, recommendation systems, and topic modeling: keep only the handful of directions that carry most of the signal, and discard the rest as an acceptable approximation. The singular value decomposition lesson later in this module covers precisely how that closest lower rank matrix gets computed.
11. Rank in Neural Network Weight Matrices

Rank shows up directly in how large language models get fine tuned cheaply today. A technique called LoRA, low rank adaptation, freezes a pretrained weight matrix entirely and learns a small correction on top of it, one built from the product of two much smaller matrices, which forces that correction itself to have low rank.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A weight matrix of size 4096 by 4096 has over 16 million entries. A rank 8 correction built from a 4096 by 8 matrix times an 8 by 4096 matrix has only about 65 thousand learnable entries, a few hundred times smaller, yet still captures the dominant directions that matter for adapting the model to a new task.

blocks.text: The underlying bet behind LoRA is precisely the low rank approximation idea from section 10: the useful adjustment a model needs for a new task rarely requires full rank freedom, a handful of dominant directions captures nearly all of the benefit at a tiny fraction of the storage and compute cost.
12. Rank and the Determinant

A square matrix has full rank exactly when its determinant is nonzero, and is rank deficient exactly when its determinant is zero. This gives a second, quick way to check the section 5 connection between rank and invertibility, since a zero determinant is precisely what makes a matrix impossible to invert.

code.content:
singular = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4]])
print(np.linalg.det(singular))            # 0.0, confirming rank deficiency
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(singular))    # 1, matching a nonzero determinant test failing

blocks.text: In practice, checking the determinant directly is a poor substitute for checking rank on anything but small matrices, since determinants of large matrices can come out as a tiny nonzero number purely from floating point rounding, even when the matrix is conceptually rank deficient. Section 13 covers this numerical caveat directly.
13. Numerical Rank and Floating Point Tolerance

Rank is defined as an exact mathematical property, but computers work in floating point, where a value that should be mathematically zero often comes out as something like 0.0000000003 due to rounding during computation. Rank-finding functions therefore do not check for exact zero, they check whether a value is smaller than a small tolerance, and treat anything below that tolerance as effectively zero.

code.content:
A = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4.0000001]])   # almost, but not exactly, rank deficient
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A))            # 1, tolerance correctly absorbs the tiny difference

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Without a tolerance, the matrix above would report rank 2, technically true to many decimal places, but practically misleading, since the two rows are for all meaningful purposes duplicates that happen to differ only due to a measurement error or rounding artifact. Numpy default tolerance scales with the matrix size and largest singular value specifically to catch cases like this.

blocks.text: 14. Rank in Data Matrices

When a dataset is arranged as a matrix, one row per sample and one column per feature, the rank of that matrix tells you how many features are actually contributing independent information, as distinct from how many columns the spreadsheet happens to have. A dataset with 50 columns but rank 12 is, informationally, a 12 dimensional dataset wearing a 50 column costume.

This is precisely why rank checks are a standard early step in a machine learning pipeline, right alongside the correlated-feature check from section 7: training a model on a rank deficient feature matrix wastes compute on redundant columns, and can actively destabilize certain algorithms, notably ordinary linear regression, which assumes the feature matrix has full column rank in order to produce a single well defined solution.
15. A Worked Example

code.content:
B = np.array([[2, 4, 6], [1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 1]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(B))   # 2, since row 1 is exactly 2 times row 2

blocks.text: It is worth spotting the dependency by eye before trusting the code output blindly, which builds the same intuition checking a determinant does for invertibility, covered in the matrix inverse lesson. Here, row 1 being exactly twice row 2 is visible directly in the numbers, without needing to run any calculation at all.
16. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a matrix rank always equals its row count or column count, it is only an upper bound, not a guarantee.
Confusing a rank-deficient matrix with an incorrectly sized one, rank deficiency is about redundant content, not a shape mismatch.
Forgetting to check rank when a matrix inversion unexpectedly fails, a low rank is one of the most common root causes.

blocks.text: 17. Practice: Find the Rank by Eye

Before running any code, look at the matrix [[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6], [0, 1, 1]] and try to spot a dependency among the rows the way section 2 and section 8 demonstrated. Once you have a guess, confirm it with np.linalg.matrix_rank().

code.content:
A = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6], [0, 1, 1]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A))   # 2, since row 2 is exactly 2 times row 1

items: Spotting the dependency by eye first builds the same intuition section 8 relies on for row space and null space.
Confirming with code afterward builds trust that the eye-spotted answer generalizes to matrices too large to inspect by hand.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

Whenever a matrix behaves unexpectedly, an inversion that fails, a regression that will not converge, a compression step that loses less quality than expected, rank is one of the first properties worth checking.

Rank counts how many truly independent rows, or columns, a matrix actually has, which can be less than its row or column count whenever some rows are just scaled combinations of others. A matrix is full rank when every row genuinely contributes new information, and rank deficient otherwise.

This single number connects directly to invertibility, a square matrix can only be inverted if it has full rank, and to the deeper idea of true dimensionality, which is exactly what the singular value decomposition and PCA lessons later in this module build on to compress and simplify data that looks larger than the information it actually contains.

Numerically, remember that rank checks on real-world, floating point data always run through a tolerance rather than an exact zero test, which is a feature, not a bug, since it correctly absorbs harmless rounding noise while still catching genuine redundancy.

Rank reappears by name in the projection, singular value decomposition, and PCA lessons still ahead in this module, each of which builds directly on the row space, column space, and null space ideas introduced here.
